newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan panel sets fiscal deficit reduction target.
newsitem.headline: Japan panel sets fiscal deficit reduction target.

text.p: An advisory panel to Japan's finance minister set a target on Thursday to reduce the government fiscal deficit to below three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2005 in an effort to balance the state budget.

The panel report, submitted to the Finance Ministry earlier on Thursday, said the government should first aim to keep spending, excluding interest payments and the redemption of government bonds, below revenues in the next two to three years.
The next step would be to keep the fiscal deficit at below three percent of GDP by 2005, which would mean at least a 0.4 percent reduction in the deficit annually, the report said.

The Paris-based Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) expects Japan's fiscal deficit for 1997 to be 6.3 percent of its gross domestic product. Japan's nominal GDP stood at 488.5 trillion yen in the year ended March 1996.
At the same time, the government should try to stop issuing deficit-financing bonds and lower its dependency on government bonds to finance the state budget.
Japan budgeted 21 trillion yen worth of government bond issues, including 12 trillion yen worth of deficit-financing bonds, to fund the core budget for the current fiscal year ending in March 1997.
The government's dependency on bonds to finance its core budget will hit 28 percent at the end of March and government bonds outstanding will total about 240 trillion yen.

The report also urged regional governments to restructure their finances. Japan's outstanding debt, including both central and regional governments, is seen accounting for about 90 percent of GDP at the end of 1996.

Ultimately, the government should aim to manage fiscal finances in a way that would not lead to an accumulation of debt and limit annual growth in both regional and central government spending to below the nation's economic growth rate, the report said.
The target to cut the fiscal deficit to below three percent of the GDP is based on the assumption that Japan's economic growth will not go over 3.5 percent annually.

Concerning a review of overall spending, the panel report said the government should review its policy of turning to public works spending as a traditional way to stimulate the economy and check this spending.

Defence spending should be kept to a minimum and official development assistance (ODA) to developing countries should also be repressed, it said. The report also urged the government to quickly come up with solutions on how to pay off about 27 trillion yen worth of debt left over by its now privatised national railway companies.

"I hope this will arouse interest and discussion among the public about fiscal reforms and move the government to tackle the issue seriously," Shoichiro Toyoda, chairman of the Fiscal System Council, told a news conference.
Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and his Liberal Democratic Party have said the government will actively tackle fiscal reforms, including submitting bills to the parliament to do so.

Another panel member told the same news conference that it was up to the LDP and the government to decide whether to include a numerical target, such as the one hammered out by the panel, in their fiscal reform bills.
"Laws to carry out fiscal reforms are one effective way of implementing them," Toyoda said.

Asked whether fiscal reforms will involve raising taxes, Toyoda said Japan must tackle deregulation which will help revitalise the economy, leading to a natural increase in tax revenues without raising taxes.
